summary: Updates RFC 6363 so the Forward Error Correction framework supports codes with a sliding encoding window as well as block codes, in a backward-compatible way. Sliding window codes help real-time multicast and broadcast content cope with loss using less repair traffic and delay.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending extra clue pieces lets a receiver rebuild lost ones. Instead of fixed batches, the clues cover a moving window, which suits live video.

questions: sliding window fec vs block fec
subtitle: Lets the FEC framework protect streaming media with a moving window of data instead of fixed blocks, cutting recovery delay.

tldr.problem: FECFRAME as defined in RFC 6363 only supports block FEC codes. Repair data cannot be produced until a whole block of source symbols exists, which adds delay for real-time flows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the framework to FEC codes with a sliding encoding window that moves over the source symbols, so repair symbols can be generated on the fly at any time. Block codes keep working, and each scheme gets its own FEC Encoding ID.
tldr.outcome: Sliding window codes can give more robustness against loss with less repair traffic and lower FEC-related latency for multicast and broadcast delivery. The RFC updates RFC 6363 and changes no packet formats.

today: RFC 8680 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2020. It updates RFC 6363 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Block Codes Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Many applications send a continuous stream of packets over networks that may lose some of them. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds repair data so a receiver can rebuild lost packets without asking for retransmission, which would add a delay that is often incompatible with real-time use. RFC 6363 defines FECFRAME, a framework for adding FEC to arbitrary packet flows over an unreliable datagram transport such as UDP. It is aimed mainly at real-time or streaming media using broadcast, multicast or on-demand delivery.

The catch is that RFC 6363 only considers block FEC schemes. These split the input flow into blocks and encode and decode each block on its own. The time needed to collect a block delays encoding, and so delays recovery at the receiver, because no repair symbol for a block can exist before the block is complete. Picking a block size is a trade-off: small blocks keep latency low, large blocks resist long loss bursts better.

This RFC updates RFC 6363 to also support sliding window FEC codes (also called convolutional codes). An encoding window, of fixed or variable size, slides over the source symbols, and repair symbols can be produced at any time from whatever is in the window. RFC 8681 is named as an example scheme built on a sliding window Random Linear Code.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting to fill a whole box before making backup copies is slow. A moving window lets you make backups continuously, so lost pieces come back faster.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC says it is fully backward compatible with RFC 6363. Block FEC codes are neither prevented nor compromised, and both kinds of code can coexist, just as different block schemes can.

Each sliding window FEC scheme gets its own FEC Encoding ID, subject to IANA registration like block schemes. Any receiver, including a legacy one that only knows block schemes, can read that ID from the FEC Framework Configuration Information. When the Session Description Protocol is used to carry it, the ID is in the encoding-id= parameter of a fec-repair-flow attribute. That lets a receiver tell whether it supports the scheme in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Old players can still read the label on the box that says which kind of backup method is inside, so they know if they can handle it.

sections.title: Key Terms Added by the Update
sections.content:
The terminology is copied from RFC 6363, with three additions. A Block FEC Code requires the input flow to be segmented into blocks, with encoding and decoding done independently per block. A Sliding Window FEC Code can generate repair symbols on the fly, at any time, from the source symbols present in the sliding encoding window at that time.

The Encoding Window is the set of source symbols at the sender that are used to generate a repair symbol. The Decoding Window is the set of received or decoded source and repair symbols at a receiver that are used to decode lost source symbols.

Other terms carry over: an Application Data Unit (ADU) is the unit of source data handed to the transport layer, a FEC Scheme defines the extra protocol aspects needed to use a particular FEC code, and the code rate is the ratio between the number of source symbols and the number of encoding symbols, always above 0 and at most 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The window is the handful of recent pieces you are using to make a clue. The sender looks at the pieces it sent, and the receiver looks at the pieces it got.

sections.title: The FECFRAME Architecture in Brief
sections.content:
The architecture of RFC 6363 applies unchanged and this RFC only summarizes it. At the sender, an application produces ADUs of variable size. Because FEC needs fixed-size symbols, a scheme-specific ADU-to-symbols mapping turns each ADU into one or more source symbols. For some schemes this prepends a length field and a flow identifier and pads to a multiple of the symbol size.

The FEC scheme then produces repair symbols. FEC Source Packets (carrying ADUs) and FEC Repair Packets (carrying repair symbols) are sent over a transport protocol that gives an unreliable datagram service. Source packets can be sent as soon as they are available, as long as a copy of the source symbols is kept for later encoding.

When several flows share one FECFRAME instance, decoded ADUs must be assigned to the right flow, since IP addresses and ports are not recovered by decoding. In some schemes each ADU is given a 1 byte flow identifier that is FEC protected along with the length, payload and padding.

Not covered: congestion control beyond high-level normative requirements, receiver feedback (which may exist inside the application, for example through RTCP), and how a sender adapts its code rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes of different sizes get chopped into same-size tiles. Each tile carries a tag so that, when a rebuilt note comes back, it goes to the right pile.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Operation
sections.content:
Packet identification works as in block codes, with a sliding window twist. A FEC Source Packet MUST carry information identifying the ADU's position in the source flow, the Source FEC Payload ID. A FEC Repair Packet MUST carry the Repair FEC Payload ID, which relates the repair payload to the source symbols used to make it. The FEC scheme defines and interprets both.

At the sender, a new ADU is passed to the FEC scheme, which updates the sliding encoding window and, if needed, returns an Explicit Source FEC Payload ID. The framework builds the source packet and sends it with the same flow identification (addresses and UDP ports) it would have had without FECFRAME. Whenever the framework needs repair packets, for instance to meet the target code rate, it asks the scheme to create repair payloads from the current encoding window together with their Repair FEC Payload IDs. The repair packets go out using the ports and multicast groups defined in the FEC Framework Configuration Information.

At the receiver, only steps 4 and 5 differ from block codes. The scheme uses the received payload IDs to place source and repair packets in the decoding window. If at least one source packet is missing and at least one repair packet has arrived, decoding is attempted. The scheme returns the received and decoded ADUs, flagging any that were missing and could not be decoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps adding new pieces to its moving window and makes clue cards from it whenever needed. The receiver uses the clue cards to fill any gaps.

sections.title: What a Sliding Window FEC Scheme Must Define
sections.content:
The packet formats of RFC 6363 stay the same, as do its rules for configuration information. The one change to the FEC scheme requirements is item (4), the full specification of the FEC code, which was specific to block codes. In its place, item 4-bis requires a full specification of the Sliding Window FEC code. It MUST precisely define the valid FEC-Scheme-Specific Information values, the valid FEC Payload ID values and the valid packet payload sizes. Given valid values for these and a valid encoding window, it MUST also uniquely define the encoding symbols in the repair payload.

A sliding window scheme additionally MUST define the mapping between ADUs and source symbols, the management of the encoding window that slides over the ADUs, and the management of the decoding window. For a linear FEC code the decoding window usually means managing a system of linear equations.

Feedback, transport protocols and congestion control are handled exactly as in sections 6, 7 and 8 of RFC 6363.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone inventing a new backup method has to write down exactly how the window moves and how a missing piece is worked out, so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.title: Hints on Managing the Window
sections.content:
Appendix A is informational. The framework does not manage the sliding encoding window; that is the scheme's job. Source symbols are added each time a new ADU has been mapped, and removed either when an old ADU of a real-time flow times out, or, once the window reaches its maximum size, by dropping the oldest symbol as each new one arrives.

Limits come from three levels: real-time constraints at the source flow level, computational complexity at the FEC code level, and signaling at the scheme level. A window made of a nonsequential set of symbols needs extra signaling to describe it, which can cap the window size. A sequential window is simpler to signal, since the first symbol's identity and the symbol count are enough, giving a fixed and relatively small overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: The window is like a conveyor belt of limited length: new items go on one end and the oldest fall off the other.

sections.title: Security, Operations and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security considerations and no new operations and management considerations, so those of RFC 6363 apply. It adds one goal to the problem statement list in RFC 6363: attacks may try to corrupt source flows in order to modify the receiver application's behavior, as opposed to just denying service.

The document has no IANA actions of its own. A scheme is identified by its FEC Encoding ID, registered in the FEC Framework (FECFRAME) FEC Encoding IDs registry under the rules of RFC 6363.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for keeping things safe are the same as before. The one new worry is that someone might tamper with the pieces to trick the receiver, not just block them.
